description: Building a crop-rotation tool from NASA 30 m field histories. Looking for: a remote-sensing/geospatial lead (HLS, Landsat or Sentinel-2 time series), a Python + web engineer, an agronomy or soil-science person (no coding needed), and a designer for data viz and the demo. Request to join with one line on what you'd bring.
summary:
Farmers choosing a crop rotation must weigh soil protection, water and a changing climate, but the evidence for their own fields is scattered across technical datasets. Field Shift turns ten seasons of NASA Earth observations into a rotation plan the farmer makes on their own priorities.

For three corn–soybean fields in Story County, Iowa, it measures from 30 m NASA HLS imagery how long the soil goes without living cover (8.2–8.5 months a year), and from NASA POWER where weather risk sits in the season: the hottest half-month, 16–31 July, falls on corn silking. Summer heat has edged up since 1981, but not significantly, so the tool plans for the year-to-year swings that already hit the crop. The farmer adds what the satellite can’t see, such as whether green after harvest was a planted cover, and every estimate updates.

Field Shift then compares staying with corn–soybean, adding a cereal rye cover, or adding oats and red clover, ordered by the farmer’s priorities, and ends with a plan: which field to start on, a season-by-season checklist, questions for the agronomist, and what the satellite record will check next season. It never predicts yield or names an optimal rotation, and it shows its checks against NASA, USDA and U.S. Drought Monitor records.
details:
What it does

It’s November, when rotation decisions are made. A farmer has three real corn–soybean fields in Story County, Iowa, chosen because the USDA Cropland Data Layer shows strict corn–soybean alternation every season from 2016 to 2025. Field Shift V2 walks them through five steps:

  1. Your farm. The three fields side by side: months a year without living cover, autumns with green after harvest, and which field to start on.
  2. What the satellite can’t see. Was each green autumn a planted cover, weeds or volunteers, or not sure? Was planting late in the seasons the satellite saw a late canopy? Can the farmer sell oats and manage spring termination of a cover? Every estimate recomputes from the answers, and each “not sure” becomes a question for the agronomist.
  3. Your season. A May–September calendar of measured heat and soil wetness from NASA POWER, with each crop’s sensitive stage laid on it: the hottest half-month, 16–31 July, falls on corn silking.
  4. Your options. Stay corn–soybean, add a cereal rye cover, or add oats and red clover, ordered by the farmer’s priorities. Each card shows measured rows (bare-soil months, years with a crop in the hottest weeks, heat and wetness in sensitive stages) and ratings better, similar or worse than today.
  5. Your plan. For the field and option the farmer picks: a season-by-season checklist, questions for the agronomist, and what the satellite record will check next season.

How it works: three deterministic engines

  1. Field history (Engine 1). About 850 NASA HLS v2.0 passes per field (Landsat plus ESA Sentinel-2, 30 m), cloud-masked with Fmask, give a per-date field NDVI. A weighted smoother rebuilds each season: green-up, peak, decline, days with and without living cover, spring green before the crop and autumn green after it. Result: about 8.2–8.5 months a year without living cover. One field shows autumn green after 4 of its 5 corn harvests, consistent with a cover crop.
  2. Stress recurrence (Engine 2). For each season it finds the crop’s sensitive window (corn silking from capped growing degree days after green-up; soybean pod set to seed fill around the greenness peak) and tests regional dryness and heat against NASA POWER’s 1991–2020 percentiles, including MERRA-2 root-zone wetness. Each count is read against a base rate: how often the same calendar window was flagged in typical years. Result: 4–5 of 10 seasons flagged per field against about 3 expected, a 16–32% chance by luck, so suggestive, not conclusive. NASA ECOSTRESS (70 m) then checks each window at field scale: it confirms the 2021 drought on all three fields, and 2020 on Field C, but not the 2022–2023 regional flags. NASA SMAP L4 root-zone moisture agrees with 7–8 of 10 dry calls per field, and the U.S. Drought Monitor shows 2022 was abnormally dry here, not drought, and records a 2020 drought we miss on two fields.
  3. Rotation comparison (Engine 3). Three options (stay corn–soybean, add a cereal rye cover, add oats and red clover) are rated better, similar or worse than the current rotation on six criteria, each with its evidence, confidence and what to verify. The cover-crop estimate uses local evidence: in nearby cover years, 0.14 less of the year went without living cover (about 1.7 months). Constraints remove options; priorities only reorder them and never change a rating.

Planning layer (V2). V2 adds a season calendar from NASA POWER: heat and root-zone wetness for each half-month from May to September, with each crop’s sensitive stage laid on it. The water rating follows those measurements: oats fill grain in June, when 31–34% of days are hot against 37–42% in the current crops’ sensitive stages and the soil is wetter, so oats keep a crop out of the hottest weeks one year in three rather than remove the risk. The farmer’s answers recompute the cover estimate live (autumns marked as weeds leave the local evidence), and the plan follows each field’s rotation phase: a rye cover goes in after corn, ahead of soybeans, so on Field C it starts after the 2027 corn harvest and on Field A a year later. V2 also answers “is it changing?”: since 1981, mid-June to mid-August highs rose 0.2–0.3 °C and 1.4–1.9 days above 30 °C per decade, and rainfall fell 6–8 mm per decade, but none of these trends is statistically significant (p ≥ 0.18), so it tells the farmer to plan for year-to-year swings rather than a steady trend. Local soil comes from USDA SSURGO: each field holds about 18.5–18.7 cm of water in the top metre, so the soil buffers short dry spells alike and does not separate the fields; it feeds the water rating’s evidence and, with slope and erodibility, the erosion rating.

Validation and limits

  • Every season keeps 16–58 clear April–October dates after cloud masking.
  • Slope from NASADEM, once smoothed, sits within 0.21 percentage points of USGS lidar; raw 30 m slope read two to three times too steep.
  • NASA SMAP L4 agrees with NASA POWER’s root-zone wetness: daily correlation 0.74–0.75 from mid-June to mid-August, and 7–8 of 10 dry calls per field (V11 passes; Field C only just).
  • Dry calls checked against the U.S. Drought Monitor for Story County: 12 of 13 fall in at least abnormally dry weeks, but only 6 reach moderate drought, and we miss the 2020 drought on two fields. We report the miss rather than retune the rule to fit it.
  • 61 automated tests: seasons with known answers, repeatable runs, priorities never changing ratings, capped growing degree days, and both web pages matching the Python engines (Field Shift V2 across all 16 combinations of the farmer’s answers).
  • Not claimed: yield or profit, soil carbon or nutrients from space, that green after harvest is a cover crop (we ask the farmer), or field-level moisture from regional data.
  • Planned rye and oat dates in the season calendar and the plan come from extension guidance (ISU, PFI, SARE), not measurement: none of the three fields has grown oats or a confirmed cover.
  • Also checked: Engine 1 green-up falls within 10 days of NASA MSLSP30NA phenology in 12 of 12 field-seasons, 2016–2019 (it runs a median 5 days early); estimated corn silking falls inside Iowa’s 25–75% silked dates from USDA Crop Progress in 12 of 15 corn seasons (the three misses are one field in late years); off-season cover calls match true-colour HLS images on 28 of 30 random dates, and 24 of 25 in a balanced set, rated blind by Claude and spot-checked by the team. All thresholds are provisional, for an agronomist to review.

Beyond Story County. NASA HLS and POWER cover farmland worldwide, so the same pipeline runs on any field. Outside the US, ISRIC SoilGrids would replace SSURGO, local crop calendars would replace USDA Crop Progress, and the crop would be read from its greenness curve instead of the Cropland Data Layer. Next steps: more rotations (alfalfa, longer small-grain rotations), an agronomist’s review of the rules, and NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 projections of future heat at silking.

Tools and technologies

Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, Shapely, pyproj) in a precompute notebook; the NASA AppEEARS API for HLS, SMAP and ECOSTRESS; the NASA POWER API; NASA Earthdata (LP DAAC) for MSLSP30NA phenology and HLS true-colour checks; Microsoft Planetary Computer for NASADEM and NAIP; USDA Soil Data Access and CroplandCROS; a Streamlit app; standalone HTML and JavaScript pages (the V1 prototype and the guided Field Shift V2 planning app); pytest; GitHub.
dataRefs: NASA HLS v2.0 (L30, S30) surface reflectance, Fmask and vegetation indices
NASA POWER daily (temperature, precipitation, root-zone wetness from GMAO MERRA-2)
NASA ECOSTRESS Evaporative Stress Index (ECO_L4T_ESI v002)
NASA SMAP L4 root-zone soil moisture (SPL4SMGP v008)
NASA MEaSUREs MSLSP30NA v011 land surface phenology (from HLS)
projectRefs: USDA NASS Cropland Data Layer, 2016–2025: crop sequence and field selection
USDA NRCS SSURGO: soil water capacity, drainage, organic matter, slope class

U.S. Drought Monitor, jointly produced by the National Drought Mitigation Center at the University of Nebraska–Lincoln, USDA and NOAA: weekly Story County statistics, 2016–2025, as a neutral check of the dry calls (V13)
USDA NASS Crop Progress, weekly Iowa corn silking, 2016–2025: check of the silking estimates (V4)
